title: Block close: the wilderness road
hookLine: slaves, sea, manna, mountain, calf, and forty years of being carried

lines: BRICKS FOR A KING WHO FORGOT.
A SEA, A MOUNTAIN, A CALF.
cards: Five weeks ago, this path opened on a people making bricks for a king who had forgotten them. Since then: two midwives who said no. A basket in the reeds.
A bush on fire that didn't burn up, and a name, I AM. Plagues, and blood on the doorposts. A sea that opened.

Thunder on a mountain, ten words, a golden calf, the back of God passing by. Corners of fields, a jubilee horn, twelve spies, a talking donkey, and an old man on Nebo looking at a land he'd never enter.
Today, a look back down that road.

teach.b: The Hebrew name for the book of Numbers is Bemidbar: in the wilderness. For these four books, that's where the people mostly are. Not in Egypt anymore, not in the land yet.
In between. They complain about the water, the food, Moses, the giants. They make a calf the moment Moses is late.
A whole generation is too afraid to go in.
Read these books looking for heroes, and almost everyone disappoints, including, at Meribah, Moses himself. But read again and notice who keeps showing up.
Manna morning after morning, even after they grumbled. Water from a rock. A pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.

Here's how Moses sums it up in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "in the wilderness, where thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place."

teach.h: CARRIED, AS A MAN BEARS HIS SON.
teach.b: Bare thee: carried you, like a father carrying a tired child on his shoulders the last mile home. That's the thread through the whole road. Not that the people were strong, or faithful, or patient.

teach.h: THE LORD THY GOD BARE THEE, AS A MAN DOTH BEAR HIS SON.
teach.b: It's that they were carried. Christians read their own lives in this road too. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, says these wilderness stories were written down as examples for later readers.

Rescued from slavery, but not home yet; fed one day at a time; failing, and carried anyway. Tomorrow the path opens the songbook those carried people and their children would one day sing: the Psalms.

how: Some Christians describe hard seasons as 'wilderness' times, and Lent's forty days recall Jesus' forty days in the wilderness, which some readers link to Israel's forty years.

the counting: a census of the twelve tribes

games.q: you're looking back over forty years in the desert: the grumbling, the calf, the fear. how does Moses sum it up?
o: the LORD bare thee, as a man doth bear his son.
you earned the land by your courage.
games.why: not the people's strength, but being carried: "the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went."

practice: Think back to an in-between stretch of your life, out of one thing and not yet into the next: a move, a job lost, an illness. Name it, then look for the manna: what kept showing up, even when you grumbled?
If you pray, thank God for carrying you; if not, thank whoever did.

wordCard.voice: Bemidbar. Hebrew for in the wilderness, the name of the book of Numbers: the long in-between where Israel was carried, not strong, from slavery to the edge of the land.
